contributions.headingText: Glomus tumour is a mesenchymal neoplasm composed of cells that resemble the perivascular modified smooth muscle cells of the normal glomus body.

2E92.1 & XH47J2 Glomus tumour, NOS, of stomach

2E92.7 & XA5DY0 & XH47J2 Glomus tumour, NOS, of liver

2F70.Z & XH5D10 Glomus tumour of uncertain malignant potential of digestive organs

2C1Z & XH21E6 Glomus tumour, malignant, of digestive organs

Glomus tumour

Acceptable: glomangioma; glomangiomyoma.

Malignant glomus tumour

Acceptable: glomangiosarcoma.

Although they occur far more commonly in superficial soft tissues, glomus tumours can rarely arise in viscera, including within the GI tract and very rarely the in liver. Within the GI tract, they virtually always arise within the stomach (particularly the antrum) and rarely within the oesophagus or small and large intestines {11859201}.

The presentation of gastrointestinal glomus tumour is with symptoms of upper gastrointestinal bleeding (haematemesis or melaena) or epigastric pain, and (less commonly) because of their antral-predominant location, symptoms of gastric outlet obstruction. Small tumours may be detected incidentally. Most tumours are solitary, but as many as 10% of patients have multiple lesions. Hepatic glomus tumours tend to be much larger than cutaneous lesions, possibly because they are less easily detectable in non-cutaneous sites {24965114;26187280}. They can present with epigastric fullness or pain, or as a mass lesion. Familial cases are rare.

These can occur at any age, but glomus tumours within the GI tract have a female predominance and a median patient age of 55 years (range: 19–90 years) {11859201}. Hepatic glomus tumours tend to arise in patients in their fourth to seventh decades of life.

Multiple familial glomus tumours occur due to inactivating mutations in GLMN, which is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Most sporadic cases are associated with NOTCH family gene rearrangements.

About half of benign and malignant glomus tumours from a variety of sites harbour recurrent NOTCH family gene rearrangements, often with fusion of NOTCH2 to MIR143 {23999936}. CARMN::NOTCH2 fusions have also been reported {35703141}. In one study, all tumours with malignant histological/clinical features showed complex copy-number alterations, including ATRX inactivation and recurrent loss of 9p21.3 (CDKN2A/B and MTAP) {35703141}.
Grossly, the tumours are well-circumscribed, often multinodular, 20–30 mm intramural masses. There may be extension into the mucosa or serosa. Cystic change and calcifications may be present.

Morphologically and immunohistochemically, GI tract glomus tumours are similar to those of peripheral soft tissue sites. They are composed of uniform, small, rounded cells with central, dark, round nuclei and moderate amounts of eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm. Individual cells are surrounded by sharply defined basal lamina. The stroma may be hyalinized and focally myxoid. Cells rarely show epithelioid or oncocytic features {7672784;3038728}.

Gastric glomus tumours can show plexiform growth within the muscularis propria. Scattered nuclear atypia and vascular invasion are relatively common, and vascular involvement is not prognostically adverse. Primary hepatic glomus tumours should be distinguished from tumours metastasizing from other sites. Most hepatic glomus tumours show conventional features.

Given the rarity of malignant tumours in the GI tract, there are limited data to define malignancy. For glomus tumours of the upper GI tract, the following features have been associated with metastatic disease: size > 50 mm and/or cytological atypia (nuclear atypia, nuclear pleomorphism, or spindled morphology) and a mitotic count of ≥ 2 mitoses/10 HPF {11859201;11145243;35703141}. This is somewhat similar to the proposed criteria for glomus tumours of all sites, which proposes the following criteria for malignancy: deep location and size > 20 mm, or atypical mitotic figures, or moderate to high nuclear grade and ≥ 5 mitoses/10 mm2 {11145243}. A subset of tumours show some, but not all, features associated with malignancy and may be considered to be of uncertain malignant potential.

There is diffuse, strong expression of SMA in virtually all cases, and caldesmon in > 60%. Most cases express type IV collagen and display net-like pericellular laminin {11859201}. There can be synaptophysin expression, a potential diagnostic pitfall in the differential diagnosis with neuroendocrine tumours (NETs), particularly in small biopsy or cytological preparations {11859201}. Chromogranin, CD56, desmin, S100, keratin, CD34, KIT (CD117), and DOG1 are negative.

EUS-guided evaluation of gastric masses may result in cytological sampling of glomus tumour. The tumour cells are usually monomorphic and round to ovoid in shape. They may resemble cells of NETs or epithelioid gastrointestinal stromal tumour. Diffuse expression of SMA helps confirm the diagnosis of glomus tumour.
Not clinically relevant, unless the tumour is malignant.

Most glomus tumours are benign, and complete resection by wedge or segmental resection or partial gastrectomy is curative. Malignant tumours are associated with the development of distant metastases and significant mortality.
